clinicalScope: Granuloma as a pathological lesion in humans, focusing on infectious and immune‑mediated causes encountered in East African and other low‑resource hospital settings.
title: Granuloma
subject: Pathology
summary: A granuloma is a small, organized collection of immune cells that forms when the body tries to wall off a substance it cannot eliminate. It can be caused by infections like tuberculosis, by immune diseases such as sarcoidosis, or by foreign material.

sections.p: Granulomas are focal aggregates of activated macrophages (epithelioid cells), often with multinucleated giant cells, surrounded by lymphocytes and a rim of fibrosis. They are classified by the presence or absence of central necrosis.
b: Caseating granuloma – central cheese‑like necrosis (e.g., Mycobacterium tuberculosis).
Non‑caseating granuloma – no necrosis (e.g., sarcoidosis, Crohn’s disease).
Foreign‑body granuloma – giant cells surrounding inert material (e.g., talc, sutures).
Necrotising (non‑caseating) granuloma – necrosis without the classic cheese appearance (e.g., certain fungal infections).

sections.p: In low‑resource settings the most common triggers are infectious agents, followed by occupational exposures and systemic immune diseases.
b: Mycobacterium tuberculosis – leading cause of caseating granulomas in Africa.
Deep fungal infections (Histoplasma capsulatum, Blastomyces dermatitidis) – especially in HIV‑positive patients.
Schistosoma mansoni eggs – cause granulomas in liver and bladder.
Sarcoidosis – non‑caseating granulomas, more common in young adults.
Beryllium exposure – occupational, mimics sarcoidosis.
Foreign material (sutures, talc, silica) – common after surgery or mining.

sections.p: Granuloma formation is a Th1‑mediated type IV hypersensitivity response that attempts to contain a persistent antigen.
b: Antigen presentation by dendritic cells to CD4+ Th1 cells.
Release of IFN‑γ and IL‑2, activating macrophages.
Macrophages transform into epithelioid cells and fuse into multinucleated giant cells.
Lymphocyte cuff forms around the core; fibroblasts lay down collagen.
If antigen persists, central necrosis may develop (caseation).

sections.p: Visible lesions vary with organ and cause; they are usually nodular, firm, and may be calcified.
b: Lung: 0.5–2 cm nodules, often peripheral; may cavitate in TB.
Liver: pale, well‑circumscribed nodules; may coalesce into larger fibrotic masses.
Skin: papules or plaques, sometimes ulcerated.
Lymph node: rubbery, non‑tender enlargement.

sections.p: The hallmark is a central core of epithelioid macrophages with or without necrosis, surrounded by a lymphocytic rim and peripheral fibrosis.
b: Langhans giant cells – peripheral arrangement of nuclei, typical for TB.
Foreign‑body giant cells – haphazard nuclei, seen with inert material.
Caseous necrosis – amorphous, eosinophilic debris, no cellular detail.
Non‑caseating granuloma – intact epithelioid cells, minimal necrosis.

sections.p: Symptoms reflect the organ involved and the underlying cause.
b: Pulmonary TB: chronic cough, night sweats, weight loss, hemoptysis.
Sarcoidosis: dyspnoea, dry cough, skin lesions, uveitis, hypercalcaemia.
Hepatic schistosomiasis: right‑upper‑quadrant pain, hepatosplenomegaly, portal hypertension.
Cutaneous foreign‑body granuloma: localized swelling, erythema, occasional discharge.

t.b: Does the image show nodules, cavitation or hilar lymphadenopathy? → Nodules with cavitation suggest TB; bilateral hilar nodes suggest sarcoidosis.
Is acid‑fast bacilli present? → Positive confirms mycobacterial infection; if unavailable, proceed to GeneXpert or clinical TB algorithm.
What is the granuloma type and are special stains needed? → Caseating granuloma + AFB = TB; non‑caseating + negative stains = sarcoidosis; foreign material visible = foreign‑body granuloma.
Is ACE elevated? → Supports sarcoidosis but not diagnostic; normal does not exclude.
Is the patient immunocompromised? → Guides suspicion for opportunistic infections (TB, fungi).

sections.p: Staging is organ‑specific; for pulmonary sarcoidosis the Scadding radiographic stages are most used.
b: Stage 0 – normal chest X‑ray.
Stage I – bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy only.
Stage II – lymphadenopathy + parenchymal infiltrates.
Stage III – parenchymal disease without lymphadenopathy.
Stage IV – pulmonary fibrosis.

sections.p: Complications arise from tissue destruction, obstruction, or systemic effects of the underlying disease.
b: Cavitary TB → haemoptysis, secondary bacterial infection.
Sarcoid fibrosis → restrictive lung disease, pulmonary hypertension.
Schistosomal hepatic granulomas → portal hypertension, variceal bleeding.
Foreign‑body granuloma → chronic pain, secondary infection.

sections.p: Therapy targets the inciting cause, modulates the immune response, and prevents organ damage.
b: Infectious granulomas – appropriate antimicrobial regimen (e.g., first‑line anti‑TB drugs).
Sarcoidosis – systemic corticosteroids for symptomatic disease; steroid‑sparing agents (methotrexate) if prolonged therapy needed.
Schistosomiasis – praziquantel single dose; treat complications (beta‑blockers for portal hypertension).
Foreign‑body granuloma – surgical excision if symptomatic; otherwise observe.

sections.p: Linking morphology to bedside findings helps narrow the differential.
b: Caseating granuloma + chronic cough → TB until proven otherwise.
Non‑caseating granuloma + erythema nodosum → consider sarcoidosis (Löfgren’s syndrome).
Granulomas with eggshell calcification on liver imaging → schistosomiasis.
Giant cells surrounding suture material on skin biopsy → foreign‑body reaction.

sections.p: When faced with a patient suspected of having a granulomatous disease, follow a structured algorithm.
b: History – exposure (TB contacts, travel, occupational), HIV status, systemic symptoms.
Examination – organ‑specific signs (lung fields, skin lesions, lymphadenopathy).
First investigations – chest X‑ray, HIV test, sputum smear if pulmonary.
If imaging shows nodules, obtain tissue biopsy when safe.
Interpret pathology in context; start empiric therapy only when diagnosis is reasonably certain.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly enlarging mass causing airway or vascular compression
Signs of disseminated TB in an immunocompromised patient

faq.a: Yes; many granulomas (e.g., sarcoid, healed TB) are non‑malignant but may cause organ dysfunction.

faq.q: Why does TB produce caseation while sarcoidosis does not?
faq.a: Mycobacterial antigens trigger a necrotising Th1 response, whereas sarcoidosis involves a more regulated immune reaction without extensive necrosis.

faq.q: What if the laboratory cannot perform special stains?
faq.a: Rely on clinical context, radiology, and empiric therapy; send specimens to a reference lab when possible.

exam: A 30‑year‑old man with chronic cough, night sweats, and a 2 cm cavitary lung nodule on X‑ray – what is the next diagnostic step and why? — Obtain sputum for acid‑fast stain and GeneXpert to confirm TB before starting therapy.

A patient with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, erythema nodosum, and normal calcium – which granulomatous disease is most likely and what test supports it? — Sarcoidosis; serum ACE may be elevated but is not required for diagnosis.

In a HIV‑positive child with abdominal pain, ultrasound shows peri‑portal hypoechoic nodules – what granulomatous cause should be considered and how to confirm? — Schistosomiasis; stool ova examination or serology, and liver biopsy if needed.
You see a skin nodule at a previous suture site; biopsy shows foreign‑body giant cells surrounding suture material – what is the management? — Observe if asymptomatic; excise if painful or infected.

A patient on long‑term steroids for sarcoidosis develops new cough and fever – what complication must you rule out? — Opportunistic infection (e.g., TB or fungal); obtain sputum cultures and consider CT chest.
How does the presence of Langhans giant cells help narrow the differential? — Their peripheral nuclear arrangement is classic for mycobacterial infection, pointing toward TB.
What radiographic stage of sarcoidosis predicts the best prognosis and why? — Stage I (bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy only) because fibrosis is absent.
When is surgical removal of a granuloma indicated? — When the lesion causes functional obstruction, persistent pain, or suspicion of malignancy that cannot be excluded by biopsy.
Explain why a negative Ziehl‑Neelsen stain does not exclude TB in a granuloma biopsy. — Sensitivity is limited; TB may be paucibacillary; culture or molecular tests are required.

A patient presents with massive haemoptysis and a known cavitary TB lesion – what immediate action is required? — Secure airway, position patient upright, and arrange urgent bronchoscopy or interventional radiology for haemostasis.
